entities.name: Hagia Sophia Church
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Hagia Sophia (Holy Wisdom) in Constantinople/Istanbul is the world's most historically significant religious building, serving consecutively as a Byzantine Christian cathedral (537-1453 CE), Ottoman imperial mosque (1453-1934 CE), secular museum (1934-2020 CE), and active mosque again (2020-present) — embodying 1,500 years of religious and political contest over the Eastern Mediterranean's holiest space. Its dome, rising 55.6 meters above the floor on a 31-meter diameter, was the world's largest for nearly a millennium, inspiring every subsequent great dome in Islamic and Christian architecture.

Justinian I commissioned Hagia Sophia after the original church was burned in the Nika Riots (532 CE). Architects Anthemios of Tralles and Isidoros of Miletus designed an unprecedented structure: a massive dome appearing to float on light through 40 windows at its base, supported by half-domes and piers in a revolutionary solution to the problem of placing a round dome on a square floor plan. 'Solomon, I have surpassed thee!' Justinian reportedly said upon entering — claiming superiority over the First Temple.

Mehmed II converted Hagia Sophia to a mosque in 1453 immediately after conquering Constantinople, adding minarets, Islamic calligraphic medallions, and covering Christian mosaics with plaster. Mustafa Kemal Atatürk converted it to a secular museum in 1934 as a symbol of modern Turkish secularism. Erdoğan's 2020 reconversion to an active mosque — greeted with prayer outside by thousands of Turkish Muslims — reversed Atatürk's secularist symbol and provoked international controversy.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Hagia Sophia's 1,500-year history as a contested sacred space — converted from cathedral to mosque to museum to mosque again — makes it the single building most expressive of the religious and political contest between Christianity and Islam over the Eastern Mediterranean.
